questions.markdown:
One of the classical examples of evolution occurs on the Galapagos Islands with Darwin finches. The islands have always been separating from the south American mainland and vary in size and elevation. The lowlands are covered with thorn scrub, while higher elevations are covered with moist and dense forests. All the organisms living on these islands are descendants of species that have migrated there, primarily from south America. In studying the finch populations, researchers have identified fourteen species, none of which are found on the mainland.

i) As opposed to the mainland, on the islands the initial flinches had the opportunity to evolve in new directions. Why?
ii) The initial finch species on the islands may have all been seed eaters, which process minimized competition as the population explained?
iii) What evidence did scientists use to determine that all fourteen species of finches on the Galapagos have one common ancestor?
